name: New South Wales
summary_text: The Conversion Practices Ban Act 2024 (No. 19 of 2024, bipartisan, in force 4 April 2025) makes practices directed at changing or suppressing sexual orientation or gender identity criminal offences punishable by up to five years' imprisonment, including taking a person interstate or overseas for the purpose or engaging a provider outside NSW. A civil complaints scheme runs through Anti-Discrimination NSW. NSW also operates an explicit self-identification prison-placement policy, reducing the risk of inappropriate custody for a detained gender-nonconforming visitor. Against these strong legal protections, NSW carries a concentrated violence pattern. Kimberley McRae was killed in her Coogee apartment (January 2020); the accused admitted killing her after learning she was transgender and the case went to murder trial (NSW Supreme Court), a positive institutional response. Mhelody Bruno, a 25-year-old Filipina trans woman who had arrived in Australia approximately six weeks earlier, was strangled; her killer received only 22 months on a consensual-strangulation account that ABC reporting showed the court never heard contested. Two killings of trans women in the same state within roughly a year, with one adequate and one clearly inadequate sentencing outcome, is recorded as a pattern plus a contested institutional response, not as isolated incidents. NSW is a common-law state with no statutory bill of rights and no state-level anti-vilification offence comparable to Victoria's 2025 criminal provision. Vs the national score of 0.86, NSW sits 0.02 below: the criminal conversion-practice ban and self-ID custody are strong positives but narrow in direct traveler-facing exposure (a typical tourist is unlikely to encounter a conversion-practice provider), while the violence-and-sentencing pattern is more relevant to a visitor's physical safety and shows both institutional capability (McRae murder trial) and institutional failure (Bruno 22-month sentence). Vs Victoria (0.88), which has the criminal vilification offence that NSW lacks, the two states trade different kinds of protection.

sources.title: Harmful LGBTQ+ conversion practices now banned in NSW | NSW Government
sources.claim_summary: NSW Government ministerial release (4 April 2025): the Conversion Practices Ban Act 2024 commenced, making conversion and suppression practices toward LGBTQ+ people (psychological or medical interventions, counselling, or sustained pressure to change or suppress sexual orientation or gender identity) a crime punishable up to five years' imprisonment, with taking a person out of NSW for the purpose carrying up to three years; a civil complaints scheme runs through Anti-Discrimination NSW with referral to NCAT; carve-outs preserve general religious teaching and parental discussion; the release also notes the Premier's apology over historical gay-convictions and government support for all 19 recommendations of the Special Commission of Inquiry into LGBTIQ hate crimes.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (state parliamentary counsel's site blocks automated fetches); the underlying record is the Conversion Practices Ban Act 2024 (No. 19 of 2024) in force 4 April 2025 as cited by the government release - the criminal and civil text the release summarises.

sources.title: Man admits to killing Sydney trans woman Kimberley McRae
sources.claim_summary: QNews report on NSW Supreme Court proceedings over Kimberley McRae, a trans woman found dead in her Coogee apartment in January 2020 (aged 69): the accused, Colombian student Hector Enrique Valencia Valencia, admitted assaulting and unlawfully killing McRae after learning she was transgender but pleaded not guilty to murder; the Crown rejected his manslaughter plea, sending the matter to a murder trial.

sources.title: Mhelody Bruno's killer was jailed for 22 months. This is the information the court never heard - ABC News
sources.claim_summary: ABC Background Briefing investigation (2 July 2021) into the killing of Mhelody Bruno, a 25-year-old Filipina transgender woman strangled in regional NSW about six weeks after arriving in Australia: her killer Rian Toyer pleaded guilty to strangulation in what he claimed was consensual sexual choking gone wrong and received only 22 months without trial; evidence never tested in court (a disturbing final video call, ambulance logs, first-responder statement, medical records, autopsy) was reviewed by a former Supreme Court judge, who said a miscarriage of justice may have occurred and the case was 'much more serious manslaughter than the Judge envisaged'.
